title: Motherboard and Chips v4.0 · chip-to-binary correlation catalog
author: Marc Lavoie
purpose: Conceptual cross-reference dataset, not physical wiring diagrams

profiles.name: CPU socket
profiles.behavior: The CPU socket itself executes no binary code. It carries processor-facing power, ground, high-speed data, reset/clock and controller signals.
profiles.signal: DDR command/address and DQ data, PCIe differential pairs, sideband signals and multiple regulated supply rails.
profiles.path: CPU package ↔ socket ↔ motherboard traces ↔ DIMM / M.2 / chipset
profiles.note: Pin assignments and signaling change with the CPU platform and socket revision.

profiles.name: Voltage regulator module
profiles.behavior: A multiphase buck regulator switches MOSFET power stages to regulate voltage. A control IC may contain digital logic, telemetry and firmware, but switching states are not general CPU instructions.
profiles.signal: Power switching, phase control, voltage/current telemetry; some controllers use PMBus or proprietary buses.
profiles.path: EPS 12 V → VRM stages → CPU power plane
profiles.note: High-current switching waveforms are analog power signals; they cannot be represented accurately by arbitrary software bits.

profiles.name: CPU EPS power connector
profiles.behavior: An EPS connector supplies DC electrical power and ground. It does not carry executable machine instructions or a general binary data stream.
profiles.signal: 12 V bulk power and return conductors.
profiles.path: PSU → EPS connector → motherboard VRM → processor
profiles.note: Do not confuse PCIe GPU power cables with EPS CPU power connectors.

profiles.name: DDR memory slots
profiles.behavior: DRAM memory chips store bit patterns as charge states and exchange data through a memory-controller protocol. The bytes are data; the DRAM chips do not execute CPU machine instructions.
profiles.signal: Clock, command/address, DQ data, DQS strobes and power; DDR5 implementations include subchannels and on-module supporting ICs.
profiles.path: CPU memory controller ↔ routed DDR channel ↔ DIMM DRAM
profiles.note: Actual DDR waveforms, training, bursts and ECC organization are much more complex than an eight-bit illustration.

profiles.name: Chipset / PCH
profiles.behavior: A platform controller hub coordinates selected I/O, storage, USB and lower-speed platform interfaces. Firmware and drivers access control/status registers through platform-defined mechanisms.
profiles.signal: PCIe, SPI flash, USB, SATA (when available), sidebands and management/control registers.
profiles.path: CPU ↔ chipset link ↔ USB / storage / firmware
profiles.note: Which controllers live in the chipset versus CPU varies widely by system.

profiles.name: PCI Express x16 slot
profiles.example: Illustrative payload: DE AD BE EF
profiles.behavior: The PCIe slot carries packets through differential serial lanes. Endpoint controllers parse transaction-layer packets; there is no instruction stream belonging to the slot itself.
profiles.signal: PCIe TLP/DLLP, link training, scrambling/encoding and lane-level electrical symbols.
profiles.path: CPU / chipset PCIe root port ↔ motherboard slot ↔ GPU / accelerator
profiles.note: The sample bytes represent arbitrary payload, not a valid complete PCIe packet.

profiles.name: PCI Express x1 slot
profiles.behavior: A smaller PCIe link uses the same layered packet architecture with fewer lanes. Device configuration and register transactions are interpreted by controllers.
profiles.signal: PCIe differential pairs, clock/reference timing and sidebands.
profiles.path: Root complex ↔ PCIe x1 slot ↔ NIC / sound / I/O card
profiles.note: Link width and speed negotiate with the device; binary data is not a CPU opcode.

profiles.name: M.2 NVMe connector
profiles.behavior: An M.2 connector may carry NVMe over PCIe. An NVMe controller processes commands using memory-resident submission/completion queues.
profiles.signal: PCIe transport plus NVMe command structures when the device and slot support it.
profiles.path: CPU/chipset → PCIe lanes → M.2 SSD controller → NAND flash
profiles.note: M.2 describes a physical form factor; some slots support SATA or other interfaces instead of NVMe.

profiles.name: Second M.2 slot
profiles.behavior: A second M.2 connector can carry PCIe/NVMe or other supported signals. Queue commands belong to the SSD controller, not to the connector.
profiles.signal: PCIe lanes, clock/reset signals, 3.3 V power; capability depends on board configuration.
profiles.path: CPU/chipset → secondary M.2 slot → SSD controller
profiles.note: Lanes may be shared with SATA/PCIe ports depending on the motherboard.

profiles.name: SATA storage ports
profiles.behavior: SATA ports transmit serialized frames to SATA devices. Host controllers format protocol structures that carry commands and data.
profiles.signal: SATA physical signaling, FIS, link primitives and frame integrity mechanisms.
profiles.path: CPU/chipset SATA controller ↔ SATA cable ↔ SSD/HDD
profiles.note: 0x27 identifies a host-to-device Register FIS type; one byte is not a complete frame.

profiles.name: 24-pin ATX power connector
profiles.behavior: The 24-pin ATX connector primarily brings supply rails and ground to the motherboard. Selected pins carry control/status logic, including power-supply enable and power-good.
profiles.signal: 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and standby rails, PWR_OK and PS_ON# signaling.
profiles.path: PSU ↔ ATX connector ↔ board regulators and loads
profiles.note: ATX power signals should not be described as general bidirectional byte streams.

profiles.name: UEFI firmware flash
profiles.behavior: A SPI NOR flash chip stores UEFI firmware bytes. During boot, the platform fetches firmware data; the flash chip accepts commands but does not itself execute x86/ARM firmware instructions.
profiles.signal: SPI clock/chip-select/data pins or other supported flash topology; command, address and data phases.
profiles.path: CPU/SoC firmware path ↔ SPI controller ↔ flash memory
profiles.note: 03h is a common SPI NOR READ opcode with a 24-bit address; actual parts may require different modes/address widths.
profiles.representation_class: Nonvolatile byte storage and command interface

profiles.name: RTC / CMOS battery
profiles.behavior: An RTC keeps time and may expose registers, sometimes using BCD encodings. The CMOS coin cell supplies standby energy, not binary data.
profiles.signal: Low-speed RTC/register access through platform logic; battery-backed timekeeping.
profiles.path: Battery → RTC power domain; CPU ↔ chipset / RTC registers
profiles.note: The specific RTC register map varies; CMOS battery is not a programmable chip.

profiles.name: Rear I/O stack
profiles.behavior: Rear I/O ports expose different controller protocols, such as USB, Ethernet and audio. Their connectors do not share a single encoding.
profiles.signal: USB packetized transfers, Ethernet frames, audio samples and display links depending on port.
profiles.path: External peripheral ↔ I/O connector ↔ controller ↔ CPU/memory
profiles.note: The example is a typical boot-protocol USB keyboard report, not generic encoding for all ports.

profiles.name: Audio codec and capacitors
profiles.behavior: An audio codec receives and emits digital audio samples, then converts them into analog voltage waveforms; it can also convert analog input into digital samples.
profiles.signal: HD Audio, I²S/TDM or other digital audio links, register controls and analog outputs.
profiles.path: Application → OS audio stack → controller → codec → speaker
profiles.note: Sample resolution, format, endianness and transport differ across devices.

profiles.name: Ethernet controller
profiles.behavior: The Ethernet controller formats link-layer frames with MAC addresses, payload type, data and error checks. A PHY converts framed information into link-specific electrical symbols.
profiles.signal: Ethernet MAC frames, preambles and FCS; PHY modulation/line coding depend on Ethernet speed.
profiles.path: CPU/memory ↔ NIC ↔ PHY ↔ twisted pair / fiber
profiles.note: 08 00 is a header field value, not a complete Ethernet packet or wire waveform.

profiles.name: Front USB header
profiles.behavior: Internal USB headers link front ports to the host controller. A USB keyboard may encode a physical key as a HID usage ID inside a report.
profiles.signal: USB transfer framing, device enumeration, endpoints and payloads.
profiles.path: Front port ↔ USB header ↔ host controller ↔ memory ↔ application
profiles.note: The HID usage value is part of a report, not the raw USB wire code.

profiles.name: Front-panel header
profiles.behavior: Front-panel power and reset buttons generally drive simple logic-level signals. Status LEDs are driven through board-level current-limited circuits.
profiles.signal: GPIO-like switch sensing and LED drive; not a general serial code stream.
profiles.path: Case switch / LED ↔ front-panel header ↔ platform control
profiles.note: Polarity and pull-up arrangement vary by motherboard.

profiles.name: Fan / pump header
profiles.behavior: A fan header may supply a PWM control signal and receive tachometer pulses. These transitions control or report fan rotation, not CPU instruction bytes.
profiles.signal: PWM duty cycle, tachometer pulse frequency, 12 V and ground.
profiles.path: Board fan controller ↔ fan / pump motor
profiles.note: PWM frequency, pinout and electrical levels must follow supported fan specification.

profiles.name: Chipset heatsink
profiles.behavior: A heatsink moves heat from chips through conduction and airflow. It is a passive thermal structure, not a binary processor or data receiver.
profiles.signal: Thermal energy, thermal resistance and airflow; no data bus inside the heatsink.
profiles.path: Chip package → thermal material → heatsink → air
profiles.note: Nearby thermal sensors are separate electronic devices.

profiles.name: Multilayer PCB stack-up
profiles.example: Differential pair ≠ a byte by itself
profiles.behavior: The PCB routes power and electrical signals between components. Copper tracks and planes are passive physical pathways; each routed signal is interpreted by its connected controller.
profiles.signal: Controlled-impedance traces, return paths, ground/power planes and vias.
profiles.path: CPU ↔ DIMM / PCIe / flash / chipset via board copper
profiles.note: Logical bits are abstractions; high-speed channels use equalization, analog waveforms and coding.

profiles.name: Reference clock generator
profiles.behavior: A reference clock generator supplies oscillating timing signals used for synchronous hardware. The waveform does not normally encode application data.
profiles.signal: Differential and single-ended clock output signals, jitter and phase.
profiles.path: Clock generator → clock buffers / controllers / device PHYs
profiles.note: A clock is a timing reference; not every transition represents a payload bit.

profiles.name: POST diagnostic display
profiles.behavior: A debug display may show hexadecimal checkpoint codes emitted during platform initialization. Those codes are diagnostic values, not generic motherboard instructions.
profiles.signal: Diagnostic I/O writes, embedded controllers, segment display drivers.
profiles.path: Firmware checkpoint → platform registers → debug display
profiles.note: POST code meanings are firmware-vendor and board-specific; 0xA2 is an example, not universal.

profiles.name: Wireless interface module
profiles.behavior: A Wi-Fi chipset constructs and decodes 802.11 frames, applies link security and modulates information onto radio carriers.
profiles.signal: 802.11 MAC frames, encryption and PHY symbols, OFDM/modulation.
profiles.path: CPU ↔ PCIe/USB/SDIO Wi-Fi interface ↔ radio ↔ antenna
profiles.note: The same payload bytes map to different over-the-air waveforms across modulation modes.

profiles.name: Power capacitors
profiles.behavior: Decoupling capacitors store electric charge and smooth supply transients near chips. They do not store application bits in the same manner as DRAM cells.
profiles.signal: Analog voltage/current over time.
profiles.path: Regulator rails ↔ decoupling capacitors ↔ chip supply pins
profiles.note: Some memory cells use capacitance to store bits; discrete board capacitors normally serve power filtering.

profiles.name: CPU processing cores
profiles.behavior: A CPU core fetches machine-code bytes, decodes instructions and executes them using registers, execution units and control logic. Implementations may internally transform instructions into micro-operations.
profiles.signal: Instruction fetch, caches, registers, arithmetic and branch/control networks.
profiles.path: System memory/cache → core fetch/decode → ALU → writeback
profiles.note: Example is x86/64 encoding; other ISAs have different instruction formats.

profiles.name: Integrated GPU / accelerator
profiles.behavior: GPU execution engines process compiled shader or compute instructions. Pixel bytes and shader instructions are distinct kinds of binary information.
profiles.signal: SIMD/SIMT execution, shader instructions, texture/VRAM/cache traffic.
profiles.path: Browser renderer → graphics API → driver → GPU → display
profiles.note: GPU instruction encodings are architecture-specific and often proprietary.

profiles.name: Last-level cache
profiles.behavior: Last-level cache stores copies of memory data along with tags, valid/dirty state and coherence-related metadata. SRAM circuitry holds the bits; cache itself does not interpret them as a program.
profiles.signal: Cache-line payloads, tags, directory/coherence signals, internal fabric traffic.
profiles.path: CPU cores ↔ cache ↔ memory controller / fabric
profiles.note: Actual line sizes, cache policies and ECC schemes vary.

profiles.name: Memory controller
profiles.behavior: The integrated memory controller schedules DRAM commands, trains timing and handles responses to memory requests. It mediates processor data/address requests into DRAM-specific signaling.
profiles.signal: DDR command/address, DQ/DQS, banks/rows/columns and refresh.
profiles.path: Core/cache ↔ memory controller ↔ motherboard DIMM routing
profiles.note: No single bit string represents READ across all DDR generations and modes.

profiles.name: On-die interconnect fabric
profiles.behavior: An on-chip interconnect transports requests, responses and data among execution cores, caches, controllers and accelerators. Encodings are implementation-defined.
profiles.signal: Addressed transactions, arbitration, flow control and optionally cache coherence.
profiles.path: CPU cores ↔ cache ↔ memory controller / PHY / GPU
profiles.note: Fabric packet formats are product-specific, not equivalent to PCIe TLPs.

profiles.name: PCIe / high-speed PHY
profiles.behavior: A high-speed PHY maps coded bit/symbol streams onto differential analog waveforms and reconstructs them at the receiver.
profiles.signal: Serial/deserializer, clock recovery, equalization, lane alignment and link training.
profiles.path: PCIe protocol engine ↔ PHY ↔ package pads ↔ motherboard copper
profiles.note: High-speed PHY voltage levels and waveforms are not rectangular TTL pulses.
profiles.representation_class: Physical signaling and PCIe link controller

profiles.name: Silicon power distribution
profiles.example: Power = voltage/current, not binary source code
profiles.behavior: Metal planes and meshes distribute supply/ground over the die. Timing and logic correctness depend on stable voltage under changing current.
profiles.signal: Analog voltage, return current, resistance/inductance and transient noise.
profiles.path: VRM → socket/package contacts → on-die power grid → logic
profiles.note: A power grid is not an address or instruction bus.

profiles.name: Clock distribution network
profiles.behavior: The clock distribution network delivers timing edges to synchronous logic. Clock-gating cells may disable local clock activity to reduce power.
profiles.signal: Clock phase, skew, jitter and gating control.
profiles.path: Clock source / PLL → clock buffers → flip-flops
profiles.note: Clock-domain crossings require synchronizers or other safe mechanisms.

profiles.name: Silicon substrate
profiles.behavior: Semiconductor processing creates transistor structures whose voltage-controlled conduction implements switching behavior. The bare substrate contains no human-readable program.
profiles.signal: Charge carriers, electric fields, doped regions and device isolation.
profiles.path: CMOS transistors → logic gates → circuits → chips
profiles.note: Binary is a logic abstraction implemented through analog semiconductor physics.

profiles.name: Metal interconnect layers
profiles.behavior: Patterned metal layers connect transistor devices into gates and functional blocks. Signal integrity, parasitics and buffering affect reliable logic timing.
profiles.signal: On-die nets, vias, buffers, interconnect capacitance and resistance.
profiles.path: Logic cell output → metal net → next cell input
profiles.note: A copper segment does not intrinsically identify whether it carries data, clock, power or control.

profiles.name: CMOS transistor devices
profiles.behavior: Complementary MOSFET devices switch to form logic gates. Large combinations produce adders, registers, decoders and controllers.
profiles.signal: Voltage-driven transistors, logic gates, flip-flops and state machines.
profiles.path: MOSFETs → NAND/NOR/NOT → registers / ALU → CPU
profiles.note: Real transistors operate continuously in voltage/current, not as perfect mathematical switches.

profiles.name: Organic package substrate
profiles.example: Signals through bump → package trace → pad
profiles.behavior: A package connects fine-pitch silicon die contacts to larger board socket/land contacts and spreads power, high-speed data and heat.
profiles.signal: Package transmission lines, power/ground, high-speed interfaces and sidebands.
profiles.path: Die bumps ↔ package traces ↔ socket ↔ motherboard PCB
profiles.note: The package is not a separately executing instruction engine.

profiles.name: Solder bumps / balls
profiles.example: Data-contact state depends on attached circuit
profiles.behavior: Solder bumps and balls carry power, ground and signal currents across device/package boundaries. The bumps are passive conductors.
profiles.signal: Electronic contact between die and package or BGA and PCB.
profiles.path: Silicon pad → solder bump → package / board pad
profiles.note: Physical contact resistance, electromigration and mechanical fatigue matter.

profiles.name: Integrated heat spreader
profiles.behavior: The heat spreader conducts thermal energy away from chip dies toward the cooler.
profiles.signal: Heat flux and thermal interface contact, not a bit protocol.
profiles.path: Die → thermal interface → metal heat spreader → cooler
profiles.note: A heat spreader does not itself decode bits or instructions.
